The decibel is a relative unit

The decibel (dB) expresses the logarithmic ratio between a quantity (such as sound pressure, voltage or power) and a reference value.

In acoustics, the usual reference is 20 μPa, the smallest sound pressure a human can hear under ideal conditions.

Sound pressure level is defined as:

where Lp is the sound pressure level (in dB SPL), p is the actual sound pressure, and p0 = 20 μPa is the reference sound pressure:

So if p<p0, the result is negative.

If ambient noise is measured at −5 dB SPL, its sound pressure is lower than the quietest sound a human can hear. In practice, a figure like this is usually the noise floor of the measuring instrument, not necessarily anything our ears can hear.

Where you meet negative decibels

  • In the recording studio: the noise level of a high-end microphone or audio device may be −100 dBV (a voltage unit).

  • In the acoustics lab: background noise is kept so low that the measured sound pressure level can fall below 0 dB SPL.

  • In audio engineering: level meters are usually referenced to 0 dBFS (full scale), so negative values mean the signal sits below the top of the available dynamic range.

Negative dB ≠ negative energy

  • It only means that a signal is smaller than the reference value.

  • In acoustics, −10 dB SPL is a sound pressure below the limit of human hearing, and usually cannot be heard.

  • In electronic audio, −60 dBFS means “close to silence.”
